item.title: Sources & interpretations
item.description:
On this paper the source question tests utility (AO3) — how useful a source is, not whether it is reliable. Judge it on two things: its content (what it shows + your own knowledge) and its provenance (who made it, when, and why). A source is never useless — even a biased or satirical one is useful evidence of attitudes.

Below is the provenance of every source AQA has set. Read it and ask: what does who/when/why tell me about how useful this is, and what is its one limitation?

item.title: Alliance System as Cause of WW1 (2019)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The Alliance System was the main cause of the First World War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the Alliance System was the main cause of the First World War. Instead, Kaiser Wilhelm II’s aggressive foreign policy of Weltpolitik had a far greater and more sustained negative impact on international relations over two decades, creating the very alliances and tensions that made war inevitable. The Alliance System and the naval arms race both played a role, but they were largely consequences of Wilhelmine aggression rather than independent causes.

item.title: American Forces and Defeat of Germany (2020)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The arrival of American forces was the main reason for the defeat of Germany in the First World War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the arrival of American forces was the main reason for the defeat of Germany in the First World War. While American troops proved decisive in 1918, the British naval blockade had spent four years systematically destroying Germany from within — starving its civilians, crippling its industry, and collapsing the morale that sustained its war effort. American forces provided the final blow, but the blockade had already broken the body Germany was fighting with.

item.title: Assassination as Cause of WW1 (2023)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand was the main reason for the start of the First World War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand was the main reason for the start of the First World War. The assassination was the trigger for the war, not its main cause. The more important reason was Kaiser Wilhelm II’s blank cheque to Austria-Hungary on 6 July 1914, which transformed a manageable Balkan crisis into a world war by guaranteeing unconditional German support for whatever action Austria-Hungary chose to take. Without the blank cheque, Austria-Hungary would almost certainly have negotiated rather than declared war.

item.title: Generals and Stalemate (2022)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The leadership of the generals was the main reason for continued stalemate on the Western Front until the end of 1917.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the leadership of the generals was the main reason for continued stalemate on the Western Front. While generals like Haig failed to adapt their tactics quickly enough, the primary reason stalemate persisted until 1917 was defensive technology — specifically the machine gun, deep dugouts, and barbed wire — which made any attack on enemy trenches catastrophically costly regardless of who gave the orders. Even a tactically brilliant general was a prisoner of the technology available to him.

item.title: Kaiser Foreign Policy as Cause of WW1 (2025)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘Kaiser Wilhelm’s foreign policy was the main reason for the start of the First World War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly agree that Kaiser Wilhelm’s foreign policy was the main reason for the start of the First World War. His policy of Weltpolitik — the ambition to make Germany a world power — systematically dismantled the diplomatic stability of Europe over twenty years, creating the very alliances, arms races, and tensions that made war probable long before any individual crisis arrived. The Alliance System and the arms race, which are often cited as independent causes, were themselves direct consequences of the Kaiser’s aggressive diplomacy.

item.title: Schlieffen Plan and Stalemate (2018)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The failure of the Schlieffen Plan was the main reason for the stalemate on the Western Front.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the failure of the Schlieffen Plan was the main reason for the stalemate on the Western Front. While its failure created the conditions for trench warfare, it was defensive technology — above all the machine gun — that sustained the stalemate for over three years. Other factors such as the failure of the Schlieffen Plan and the leadership of generals contributed, but they lacked the persistent, decisive power of technology in making any offensive breakthrough impossible.

item.title: Schlieffen Plan and Western Front Duration (2024)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The failure of the Schlieffen Plan was the main reason why the fighting on the Western Front lasted so long.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the failure of the Schlieffen Plan was the main reason why fighting on the Western Front lasted so long. Its failure created the conditions for trench warfare, but the primary reason fighting lasted four years was defensive technology — the machine gun above all — which gave defenders such an overwhelming advantage that neither side could break through until tanks and new tactics shifted the balance in 1917–18. The Schlieffen Plan’s failure was the starting pistol; the machine gun was the wall neither side could climb.

item.title: Spring Offensive and End of WW1 (2021)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2 · +4 SPaG

The question

‘The failure of Ludendorff’s Spring Offensive was the main reason for the end of the First World War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [16 + 4 SPaG marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly disagree that the failure of Ludendorff’s Spring Offensive was the main reason for the end of the First World War. While the failure of the Spring Offensive left Germany critically weakened, it was the collapse of German society from within — driven by the prolonged impact of the British naval blockade — that made the end of the war unavoidable. The Spring Offensive’s failure was the turning point on the battlefield; the blockade was the reason Germany could no longer sustain the fight.

item.title: Balkans 1908 09 (2020)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying the Balkans in 1908–1909? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying the Balkans in 1908–1909 because it is a direct communication between the Emperor of Austria and Kaiser Wilhelm II, written in September 1908 at the moment when Austria-Hungary was planning to announce the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This gives historians direct access to the thinking of the Austro-Hungarian leadership and the nature of its relationship with Germany at a critical moment. The letter reveals how Austria-Hungary sought German backing before taking action, and how the alliance between the two empires functioned in practice. The provenance of Source B makes it exceptionally valuable — as a private diplomatic letter between heads of state, it is not propaganda or public posturing; it reflects the genuine strategic calculations and concerns of the two empires’ leadership, giving historians insight into decision-making at the highest level.

item.title: Defeat Germany 1918 (2018)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying the reasons for the defeat of Germany in 1918? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying the reasons for the defeat of Germany in 1918 because it reveals the devastating impact of the British naval blockade on German civilian life. Princess Blücher’s diaries, written from inside Germany in 1917–18, describe the deteriorating conditions that Germans endured — food shortages, collapsing morale, and the growing sense that the war was unwinnable. This is useful because historians know that Germany’s civilian collapse in late 1918 — the mutinies, the workers’ councils, the Kaiser’s abdication — was as significant as any military defeat. The provenance of Source B is particularly valuable: Blücher was an Englishwoman living inside Germany, giving her an unusual dual perspective — she could observe German society from the inside without the bias of a German nationalist. Her diaries were written as a private record, not government propaganda, which makes them a credible account of genuine civilian suffering.

item.title: End Ww1 (2022)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying the end of the First World War? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying the end of the First World War because it shows the significance of American entry into the war for Allied morale in 1917. The poster’s exclamation ‘Here come the Americans!’ and the image of a massive American figure towering over a small German soldier captures the enormous psychological boost that America’s entry into the war gave to the French public after three years of devastating losses at Verdun and the Somme. America’s declaration of war in April 1917 also had practical significance — it meant that approximately two million fresh American troops would eventually arrive on the Western Front, directly offsetting Russia’s withdrawal and giving the Allies a decisive material advantage. The provenance of Source B as a French propaganda poster from 1917 is significant — its purpose was to sustain French civilian morale at a moment of crisis, when French army mutinies after the Nivelle Offensive had severely undermined fighting capacity. It shows what France most needed to believe about the future of the war.

item.title: Germany Britain Rivalry (2021)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying the rivalry between Germany and Britain before the First World War? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying the Germany-Britain rivalry because it is a direct statement of intent by the Kaiser himself, addressed to young German sailors in 1901. A speech by the Kaiser to naval recruits at the start of Germany’s Dreadnought-building programme would have set out Germany’s naval ambitions in explicit terms, revealing why Germany was building a large battle fleet and what it hoped to achieve. This is useful because the naval arms race was the most direct and visible expression of the rivalry between Germany and Britain, and the Kaiser’s own words provide the clearest evidence of German intent. The provenance of Source B as a speech by Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1901 is historically significant — as Commander-in-Chief of the German armed forces, the Kaiser’s statements carried the full authority of the German state, making this a primary expression of German foreign policy ambition.

item.title: Military Tech Tactics (2019)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying military technology and tactics in the First World War? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying military technology and tactics because it shows the ‘creeping barrage’ tactic in action — British soldiers advancing behind a moving curtain of artillery fire. This tactic was developed from 1916 onwards to provide infantry with cover as they crossed no-man’s-land, addressing the fundamental problem that had caused such catastrophic casualties in earlier battles like the Somme. The visual representation of soldiers advancing in formation behind the barrage is useful for understanding how commanders tried to coordinate infantry and artillery, reducing the gap between the end of shelling and the start of the infantry attack. The provenance of Source B as a British newspaper photograph from October 1917 is worth noting — published images were subject to wartime censorship and were approved by military authorities, meaning this image was intended to show the British public that the army had adapted its methods, though it may not have shown the full picture of the human cost involved.

item.title: Spring Offensive (2024)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying Ludendorff’s German Spring Offensive? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying the Spring Offensive because it is a first-hand account from a German army officer who fought on the Western Front in 1918. Such an account would provide historians with direct insight into the experience of the Spring Offensive from the German perspective — the innovative stormtrooper tactics used, the initial dramatic advances, and ultimately why the offensive failed to achieve its objectives. German officers’ accounts are particularly valuable for understanding the operational reality of the offensive, since they were positioned to observe both the tactical successes and the logistical failures (supply lines could not keep pace with the advance) that ultimately doomed it. The provenance of Source B as a first-hand military account gives it high credibility for operational detail, though the officer’s personal perspective means it may not capture the full strategic picture — it reflects one participant’s experience rather than the command decisions of Ludendorff himself.

item.title: War At Sea (2023)
item.description:
12-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

How useful are Sources B and C to an historian studying the war at sea? Explain your answer using Sources B and C and your contextual knowledge. [12 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Source B is useful to an historian studying the war at sea because it is an official internal document from the German naval leadership, revealing the strategic thinking behind Germany’s decision to resume unrestricted submarine warfare. The German navy’s request to the Kaiser in December 1916 shows that Germany’s naval commanders believed submarine warfare offered a way to win the war by starving Britain into surrender before America could intervene. This is useful because it illuminates the decision-making that led to one of the war’s most consequential choices — a decision that ultimately brought the United States into the conflict. The provenance of Source B as an official government document is extremely valuable: unlike propaganda, it was not intended for public consumption, meaning it reflects the genuine strategic calculation of Germany’s naval commanders rather than a version shaped for public reassurance. It shows that Germany was aware of the risk of provoking America but calculated the gamble was worth taking.

item.title: Alliance System and Spread of Conflict (2022)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the Alliance System contributed to the spread of conflict in 1914. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which the Alliance System contributed to the spread of conflict in 1914 was by turning an Austro-Serbian dispute into a European war within days. When Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, Russia mobilised in support of Serbia — Russia had promised in 1909 it would never again back down in a Balkan crisis, as it had done in humiliation during the Bosnian Crisis. Germany, bound by the Triple Alliance and having given Austria-Hungary its blank cheque, declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, honouring its alliance obligations. France was drawn in through the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894. As a result, a localised Balkan conflict between two states had spread to engulf all major continental European powers in under a week.

item.title: America Enters WW1 (2023)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the entry of America had an impact on the First World War. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which America’s entry had an impact on the First World War was that it provided the Allies with a decisive injection of fresh manpower and resources at a critical moment. When Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, American ships were sunk and American lives were lost. The interception of the Zimmermann Telegram — in which Germany proposed that Mexico attack the United States — further inflamed American public opinion. President Wilson asked Congress to declare war on Germany on 6 April 1917. By 1918, approximately two million American troops had arrived on the Western Front, directly offsetting the loss of Russia following the Bolshevik Revolution. As a result, the Allies, who had been fighting a war of attrition for three years, gained the numerical and material advantage needed to mount offensive operations.

item.title: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand (2021)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand led to the outbreak of the First World War. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which the assassination of Franz Ferdinand led to the outbreak of the First World War was by giving Austria-Hungary a pretext to destroy Serbia. On 28 June 1914, Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was shot in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip of the Black Hand, a Serbian nationalist group. Austria-Hungary blamed the Serbian government directly and, backed by Germany’s ‘blank cheque’ guarantee of unconditional support issued on 6 July, delivered a ten-point ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July. Serbia accepted nine of the ten points but refused to allow Austro-Hungarian officials to conduct an investigation on Serbian soil. This gave Austria-Hungary the justification it had sought, and it declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914. As a result, the assassination transformed a long-standing Austro-Serbian rivalry into an active armed conflict.

item.title: Balkans Crisis 1908 (2018)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how events in the Balkans in 1908 became an international crisis. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which events in the Balkans in 1908 became an international crisis was Austria-Hungary’s annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In October 1908, Austria-Hungary formally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, a province it had administered since 1878 but had never formally controlled. This enraged Serbia, which had expected eventually to absorb the territory itself given Bosnia’s large Slavic population. Serbia mobilised its army and demanded compensation, leading to a direct confrontation between Austria-Hungary and Serbia. Russia, which saw itself as the protector of Slavic peoples in the Balkans, supported Serbia’s protests and began diplomatic mobilisation. As a result, what had begun as an Austro-Hungarian internal decision rapidly escalated into a confrontation involving two rival European power blocs.

item.title: Russia Withdrawal (2025)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the First World War was affected by Russia’s withdrawal from the fighting. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which the First World War was affected by Russia’s withdrawal was that it allowed Germany to transfer over one million troops from the Eastern Front to the Western Front. The Bolshevik Revolution of October 1917 brought Lenin to power on a platform of ‘Peace, Land, Bread’. The Provisional Government had continued fighting, but Lenin immediately opened peace negotiations with Germany. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918, ended Russia’s involvement in the war and surrendered vast territories including Ukraine, Poland, and the Baltic states. As a result, Germany was no longer fighting on two fronts and could concentrate its forces in the west, giving it a temporary numerical advantage over the British and French for the first time since 1914.

item.title: Schlieffen Plan Problems (2019)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the Schlieffen Plan led to problems in 1914. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which the Schlieffen Plan led to problems in 1914 was that it required Germany to march through Belgium, which brought Britain into the war. The Plan, devised in 1905 by Chief of Staff Alfred von Schlieffen, assumed Belgium would allow German troops passage to attack France from the north. However, Belgium refused and resisted the German advance, slowing it significantly. This was not merely a military setback — it activated the 1839 Treaty of London, which guaranteed Belgian neutrality and obligated Britain to defend it. Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914. As a result, what had been a continental war between the major powers became a global conflict involving the world’s greatest naval power, transforming the nature and scale of the war.

item.title: Trench Warfare and War of Attrition (2020)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how trench warfare on the Western Front led to a war of attrition. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which trench warfare on the Western Front led to a war of attrition was that defensive technology made any offensive attack extraordinarily costly. Once both sides had dug continuous trench lines stretching over 400 miles from the English Channel to Switzerland by late 1914, the machine gun became the dominant weapon. A single machine gun could fire up to 600 rounds per minute, cutting down advancing infantry before they could cross no-man’s-land. Barbed wire further slowed attackers and funnelled them into killing grounds. This meant that the attacking side always suffered far greater casualties than the defender. As a result, commanders on both sides accepted that breakthrough was impossible and instead focused on wearing down the enemy’s manpower — a strategy of attrition rather than movement.

item.title: War at Sea (2024)
item.description:
8-mark question · Narrative account · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the war at sea affected the First World War. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which the war at sea affected the First World War was through the British naval blockade, which systematically destroyed Germany’s ability to sustain the war effort. From August 1914, the Royal Navy enforced a blockade of German ports, preventing food, raw materials, and military supplies from reaching Germany by sea. By 1917, German civilian rations had fallen to just 1,000 calories per day — less than half of what a person needs. Approximately 750,000 German civilians died from malnutrition and related illness during the war. Industrial production suffered as imported raw materials dried up. As a result, the blockade steadily undermined German morale and productive capacity, contributing directly to the collapse of civilian support for the war and the revolution that overthrew the Kaiser in November 1918.
